articles.summary: Has there ever been a good movie about climate change? The Day After Tomorrow , from the filmmakers behind Independence Day , was hokey disaster schlock; Don't Look Up , from the director of T he Big Short , was a relentlessly cringey metaphor movie; the little-seen How To Blow Up a Pipeline was somewhat better, but its intendedly sympathetic tale of climate radicalism was an own goal that inadvertently indicted its activist-terrorists as neurotic whack jobs. Interstellar and Project Hail Mary are much better films by any measure, but their status as "climate cinema" is at least arguable. And they are, rather notably, about the importance and vitality of risk taking and human ingenuity in the face of civilizational challenges, not pious lectures about consumption, capitalism, and environmental doom. Smug, self-satisfied lectures about human depravity generally don't make for great movies. Turns out that's true even with a top-tier director and the world's biggest movie star. Digger , the new movie from director Alejandro G. Iñárritu and star Tom Cruise, is a spectacular misfire, conceptually bold and occasionally intriguing, but mostly just an exercise in teeth-grinding awfulness.

articles.author: Hank Berrien
articles.summary: Paris is burning, but this time, the kids are holding the matches. What started as a teenage tantrum over hot classrooms and missing teachers has exploded into full-blown chaos across France. Masked high school students and leftist agitators have turned Parisian schools and suburban schoolyards into war zones, hurling Molotovs, torching entrance halls, and fighting with riot police. By Friday, the riots had crippled the nation’s education system. Government officials reported that education at more than 560 high schools had been completely shut down or disrupted, according to AFP. On Thursday, nearly 1,000 schools had been affected, with more than 160 forced to lock their doors entirely as violence spread from the working-class Parisian suburbs to major hubs like Marseille, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, and Lille. The chaos even spilled across the border into Belgium, where teens targeted classrooms in Liège. stories.summary: The US labor market added 29,000 jobs in September, falling far short of economists’ expectations following a strong showing in August, and the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2%. Downward revisions for July and August also point to a weaker labor market than first though. The report adds to evidence that the Federal Reserve will hold rates steady at its October meeting. Traders in fed funds futures curtailed bets on a Fed rate hike , per CME Fedwatch, and the 10-year Treasury yield slid about 6 basis points after nearing its highest level since 2002.
